# Asubhānupassī Sutta (Iti 85 (It 3.36 PTS It 80))

**ID:** Iti 85 (It 3.36 PTS It 80)
**Section:** Itivuttaka (iti)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Asubhānupassī Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0504m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Asubhānupassī Sutta* ("Observing Ugliness", Iti 85; PTS It 80–81) is a discourse in the *Tikanipāta* (Book of the Threes) of the *Itivuttaka*. In this sutta, the Buddha enjoins the monastics to undertake three coordinated practices: dwelling in the contemplation of bodily foulness (*asubhānupassī kāyasmiṃ*), keeping mindfulness of breathing well established internally before oneself (*ānāpānassati*), and dwelling in the contemplation of impermanence across all conditioned phenomena (*sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccānupassino*) [Ñāṇamoli 1952; Wen]. The discourse outlines the direct results of each practice: contemplating bodily foulness abandons the underlying tendency to lust for the element of beauty (*subhāya dhātuyā rāgānusayo*); properly establishing mindfulness of breathing eliminates external discursive thoughts associated with distress; and contemplating the impermanence of all conditioned formations eradicates ignorance (*avijjā*) and brings about knowledge (*vijjā*) [Ñāṇamoli 1952; Wen].

In secondary scholarship and meditation literature, the sutta is cited as an important canonical treatment of mindfulness of breathing and insight [Sarao and Long 2017; Ñāṇamoli 1952]. Tzungkuen Wen highlights the exegesis in the *Itivuttaka* commentary (*Paramatthadīpanī* II 89), which notes that while contemplation of foulness and breath meditation involve both serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), the contemplation of impermanence serves as a "pure insight meditation subject" (*suddhavipassanākammaṭṭhāna*) suited to dry-insight practitioners, dismantling the ignorance that conceals the true nature of reality [Wen].

 Algorithmic text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus registers no cross-language matches scoring 10 or above, but identifies extensive internal reuse within the *Itivuttaka* (34 matches across 8 texts), sharing substantial formulaic segments with the *Nissaraṇiya Sutta* (Iti 72, §2.7–5.1 ↔ §2.5–5.1), *Dutiyavedanā Sutta* (Iti 53, §3.4–5.1 ↔ §3.4–5.1), and introductory and concluding phrasing with Iti 55, Iti 86, Iti 87, and Iti 95 [DharmaNexus].
